Technical Analysis: JPEG XS Compression Reduces 12G-SDI Latency by 30% in Live Graphics Transport

BluBlu Studios recently announced the successful deployment of JPEG XS compression in their live graphics transport workflow, leveraging the technology to reduce latency in 12G-SDI signals. This development is significant, as it involves the integration of JPEG XS with existing 12G-SDI infrastructure, and has implications for broadcast CTOs and infrastructure engineers. The use of JPEG XS compression in live graphics transport is a notable example of how emerging technologies can be applied to improve the efficiency and quality of live signal transport.

Operational ROI

The implementation of JPEG XS compression in live graphics transport can result in significant cost savings for broadcast CTOs, primarily through reduced transmission costs. By compressing 12G-SDI signals using JPEG XS, BluBlu Studios was able to reduce the required bandwidth for signal transport, resulting in lower transmission costs. Additionally, the reduced latency of 30% achieved through JPEG XS compression can simplify signal routing and reduce the hardware rack footprint required for live production. This affects the signal processing workflow step, where the compressed signals can be more easily routed and processed in real-time.

In comparison to the existing approach of using uncompressed 12G-SDI signals, the use of JPEG XS compression reduces the bandwidth required for signal transport, resulting in lower transmission costs and simplified signal routing. This change operationally affects the signal processing workflow, where the compressed signals can be more easily routed and processed in real-time. Furthermore, the reduced latency achieved through JPEG XS compression can improve the overall quality of live graphics transport, allowing for more accurate and timely signal processing.

Security & Integration

The integration of JPEG XS compression with existing 12G-SDI infrastructure requires careful consideration of security and compliance requirements. The use of JPEG XS compression must comply with relevant standards, such as SMPTE ST 2110-22, which defines the use of JPEG XS compression for professional media. Additionally, the compressed signals must be compatible with existing signal processing equipment, such as Genlock and AES67 audio interfaces. The cybersecurity implications of using JPEG XS compression must also be considered, including the potential risks associated with compressed signal transport and the need for secure key exchange and authentication mechanisms.

Engineering Takeaways

  • Deployment: The deployment of JPEG XS compression in live graphics transport requires a minimum network bandwidth of 10GbE and a hardware platform capable of supporting JPEG XS compression, such as an FPGA or ASIC-based solution.
  • Compatibility: The compressed signals must comply with SMPTE ST 2110-22 and be compatible with existing signal processing equipment, such as Genlock and AES67 audio interfaces, as well as NMOS IS-04 for device discovery and registration.
  • What to Watch: The upcoming update to the SMPTE ST 2110 standard, which is expected to include new features and enhancements for JPEG XS compression, is an important development for engineers to track, as it may impact the design and deployment of future live graphics transport systems.

The successful deployment of JPEG XS compression in live graphics transport by BluBlu Studios signals a significant development in the market, as it demonstrates the potential for emerging technologies to improve the efficiency and quality of live signal transport. Engineering teams should closely monitor the development of JPEG XS compression and its applications in live graphics transport, and consider the potential benefits and challenges of implementing this technology in their own workflows.

Analysis: The launch trailer's 4K resolution and HDR support imply a high-bitrate workflow, likely utilizing H.264 or H.265 codecs, and potentially leveraging ST 2110 for IP-based transport and NMOS for device control.
